values.name: exampleMotor
values.value: 400 V, 50 Hz, four-pole (1500 rpm field speed), base frequency 50 Hz
values.why: The lesson needs one motor to drag the frequency on. 400 V and 50 Hz are the usual UK three-phase supply and the brief's choice; a four-pole motor matches lesson 1's recall question. It is an example motor, not a maker's rating. Every other number on the picture (8 V per Hz, field speed 120 f ÷ p, flux) is computed from these three.
values.realValueLives: The motor's rating plate: rated voltage, rated frequency, pole count (and the maker's data sheet for rated speed).

values.name: fanRatedPower
values.why: The fan-load switch needs a full-speed power to scale by the cube law (0.75 cubed is about 42%, 0.5 cubed is 12.5%, computed from the sourced rule). 11 kW is a plausible ship's ventilation fan size and only an example; the lesson also shows the result as a percentage of full power so nothing depends on the kW figure.
values.realValueLives: The fan's data plate or the maker's fan curve at the duty point; the cube law is an ideal that real systems only approach (ABB: treat the savings as theoretical).

values.name: lowSpeedCoolingWarningFrequency
values.why: The picture warns when a standard self-cooled motor is run slowly under a heavy load. Sources say only that a self-ventilated motor cools less as it slows and its continuous torque at low speed is limited; none gives a frequency. 20 Hz is a labelled example threshold for the picture's warning and is never shown as a rule.
values.realValueLives: The motor maker's thermal loadability (derating) curve against speed, or the drive and motor maker's selection guide.

values.name: fastStopRampAndBusRise
values.value: fast ramp 2 s: DC bus rises from 540 V to 700 V; slow ramp 30 s: stays near 540 V
values.why: The fault check ('trips every time a big fan is stopped quickly') is taught with a bus-voltage gauge. The sources give the cause (energy returned to the DC bus when slowing a high-inertia load, fixed by a longer deceleration time or a brake chopper) and give the resting bus as 1.35 times the supply volts (540 V on 400 V, computed) and one maker's overvoltage trip at 840 V for a 400 V drive. They give no ramp times or peak. 2 s, 30 s and 700 V are example numbers, drawn clearly below the 840 V trip line, labelled as an example drive.
values.realValueLives: The drive's own parameters (deceleration time, overvoltage trip level, brake chopper) in its manual, and the load's inertia.

values.name: dcBusAfterIsolation
values.why: Computed, not invented: nominal DC link voltage is the supply line voltage times 1.35 (ABB ACS800 hardware manual), so 400 V gives 540 V (the same manual also gives 1.41, about 564 V). Shown as 'roughly 540 V' so the safety screen says why waiting 5 minutes and measuring matters. Keep as a computed value, not a maker's figure for any one drive.
values.realValueLives: Measure UDC+ to UDC- on the drive itself; the drive manual gives the wait time (ABB: 5 minutes) and the test points.

values.name: aboveBaseSpeedValues
values.value: at 60 Hz: field speed 1800 rpm, flux 83% of rated (50 ÷ 60), torque about 83% of rated at constant power
values.why: Computed from the sourced rules (field speed 120 f ÷ p; volts stop rising at base frequency so flux falls as 1 ÷ f; constant-power region). The 83% figures are the ideal textbook trend, not any drive's measured curve, and are labelled as the ideal. The sources do not give per-unit curves.
values.realValueLives: The motor's and drive's torque-speed capability curve in the maker's data.
